messages.subject_clean: multistate dynamic occupancy - troubleshooting model initiation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all. I am having trouble with a couple issues trying to initiate the attached model. Would greatly appreciate any assistance helping me see what I'm doing wrong. In addition to the model code, I've attached the R objects that I'm feeding to nimble. Once these files are located in the designated workspace, running the following should replicate what I am seeing:

source("MultiStateOcc_dynamic_habitat.nimble")
params <- R.utils::loadObject("params")
inits <- R.utils::loadObject("inits")
constants.inp <- R.utils::loadObject(" constants.inp  ")
data.inp <- R.utils::loadObject("data.inp")
model <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model", constants = constants.inp,
                       data = data.inp, inits = inits)

Issues:
1. In the course of initialization, I get "Error in inprod(model$beta.psi[1:2] * model$X.hab[getNodeFunctionIndexedInfo(INDEXEDNODEINFO_, :
argument "v2" is missing, with no default". Am I erring in how I am using 'inprod'? The model code line referenced in the error is line 30, but I'm also not getting phi or rho to initialize (lines 41-44). I am providing values for beta.psi and X.hab. After running the initialization, `model$beta.psi` returns '0  0' and `sum(is.na <http://is.na>(model$X.hab))` returns '0'.
2. The second and (apparently) independent issue is that I am not getting 'z.pair' to initialize (line 61). I tried specifying this node first with 'z.pair[j] <- (z[site.ind[j], year.ind[j]] == 3)' and now as 'z.pair[j] <- step(z[site.ind[j], year.ind[j]] - 2.5)'. Neither appears to work even though I am providing initial values for 'z'.

One thing I am wondering is if my constants are not getting sent to the model properly. I can't seem to see any of the constants I've provided in the model object (e.g., 'model$k.hab' and 'model$nsurveys' don't return anything), although I don't remember trying to look for these specifically in the past, i.e., not sure if constants are held in the model in the same way that data objects and variables are.

messages.subject: Returning full log-likelihood from NIMBLE
messages.subject_clean: Returning full log-likelihood from NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I was wondering if there was a way to return the full un-normalised log-posterior densities for each iteration of the MCMC from NIMBLE (essentially as a way of monitoring convergence)? I know that getLogProbs() will extract the latest value for single nodes, but I want the value at each iterations summed across all nodes. Is this possible to get easily?

Many thanks,

TJ

Many Thanks,

Philip

messages.subject_clean: missing values in two response (joint model)
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Dan. The data I have is attached. I am wondering if I can delete those NA case from response manually(only consider the non-NA) case.  But I always have the errors and I am not sure how to fix that. THanks!!

library(scales)
library(MCMCvis)
library(nimble)
library(MASS)
library(writexl)
library(readxl)
library(grid)
library(dplyr)
library(data.table)

y_NA=fread("missing_response.csv")
setDF(y_NA)
vec1=colSums(!is.na <http://is.na>(t(y_NA)))
vec1=c(0,vec1)
vec1=as.vector(vec1)

loc=which(!is.na <http://is.na>(y_NA),arr.ind = T)
loc=data.frame(loc)
colnames(loc)=c("person","item")
try=loc %>%
  group_by(person) %>%
  summarise(score = list(item))

trytry=try[[2]]
vec2=as.vector(unlist(trytry))

y=c(t(y_NA))
y=na.omit(y)

#model we fit
code=nimbleCode({
  for (n in 1:1000) {
    for (i in 1:vec1[n+1]) {
      add=vec1[n]
      index=vec2[add+i]
      for (k in 1:7) {w[n, index, k] <- pow(attribute[n, k], Q[index, k])}
      logit(prob[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]]) <- beta[index] + delta[index] * prod(w[n,index, 1:7])
      y[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]] ~ dbern(prob[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]])
    }}
  for (n in 1:1000) {
    for (k in 1:7) {
      logit(att_prob[n, k]) <- gamma[k] * theta[n] - lambda[k]
      attribute[n, k] ~ dbern(att_prob[n, k])
    }}

  for (n in 1:1000) {theta[n]~ dnorm(0,1)}
  for (i in 1:30) {
    item_parameter[i, 1:2] ~ dmnorm(item_mu[1:2], item_den[1:2, 1:2])

    beta[i] <- item_parameter[i, 1]
    delta[i] <- item_parameter[i, 2]
  }

  for (k in 1:7) {
    lambda[k] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    gamma[k] ~ T(dnorm(0, 1),0,)

  }
  item_mu[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  item_mu[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, 1),0,)

  R[1, 1] <- 1
  R[2, 2] <- 1
  R[1, 2] <- 0
  R[2, 1] <- 0
  item_den[1:2, 1:2] ~ dwish(R[1:2, 1:2], 2)
})

data <- list(y=y,Q=Q,vec1=vec1,vec2=vec2)
inits <- list(item_den = diag(2))
monitors=c("gamma","lambda","beta","delta")
model<-nimbleModel(code,data = data,inits=inits)
cModel_DINA <-compileNimble(model)
conf_DINA <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = monitors)
model_DINAMCMC <- buildMCMC(conf_DINA)
cModel_DINAMCMC <- compileNimble(model_DINAMCMC, project = model)
system.time(samples_DINA<-runMCMC(cModel_DINAMCMC, nchains=2,niter = 100, nburnin = 10))

messages.subject: compilation of sampler; getParam, object 'i' not found
messages.subject_clean: compilation of sampler; getParam, object 'i' not found
messages.body_plain:
Hello again,

In my attempt to code up a sampler, I encountered this error. Depending on how I code things the error varies, sometimes it is "i" not found (as in the attached example), in other cases it might be "parameter cov not found in distribution dnorm", or "parameter 'NA' not found in distribution". It seems I am misunderstanding how NIMBLE approaches this problem.

Essentially, the sampler I am writing is suitable for models with normally distributed priors, and on each iteration requires constructing the prior covariance matrix across all priors. To do so, I check if a prior has a normal or multivariate normal distribution, and retrieve the appropriate hyperparameter by either itsr index slot.

So, in the "setup" code I check each parameter its distribution, and store the index of the appropriate hyperparameter slot in an integer vector. When accessing the "run" code in the model directly this works fine, but when compiling the sampler I run into issues.

Attached a minimum reproducible example, I am grateful for any suggestions on what I might be doing wrong here, and suggestions on how to approach this issue instead.

Kind regards,
Bert

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a Gaussian Process model, and I would like to include the output of this model as a linear factor in a GLM.  As part of my workflow, I have already defined the basic format of the GLM as a `nimbleCode`, and I have defined the GP as a `nimbleCode` as well.  It would be super nice if there were some way to create a new `nimbleCode` that does something vaguely like:
```
    covariates <- stack(matrixOfCovariates, myGPModel["s"])
    myGLMModel["lambda"] <- rowSum(covariates)
```
Basically, the desire is to not have to copy-pasta my code into a huge wall of a model, when the GLM and the GP are already defined, and the tie between them is this single additive bit.

Is there any way to combine multiple individual models into a "large" model?

Cheers,
-Scott!

messages.subject_clean: compilation of sampler; getParam, object 'i' not found
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bert,

`getParam` is designed to work with the second arg being the character string name of a parameter, not a position in the set of arguments,
i.e., getParam('y', 'var') not getParam('y', 2). You're doing the latter.

Behind the scenes, we do map strings to numeric indexes internally. And in this case I think that is causing the behavior you are seeing. Here's an illustrative example showing the mapping in the case of `dnorm`:

code <- nimbleCode({
    y ~ dnorm(5, sd = 10)
})
m  <- nimbleModel(code, inits = list(y = 3))

m$getParam('y', 1)  # value of y
m$getParam('y', 2)  # mean
m$getParam('y', 3)  # sd
m$getParam('y', 4)  # precision
m$getParam('y', 5)  # var

[1] 3
[1] 5
[1] 10
[1] 0.01
[1] 100

I think that will allow you to work through the errors/behavior you are getting.

You may be able to hack something that works uncompiled using indices rather than strings as the second argument, but I haven't looked to see what will happen if you try to compile that.

Happy to iterate on this.

-chris

> `getParam` is designed to work with the second arg being the character string name of a parameter, not a position in the set of arguments,
> i.e., getParam('y', 'var') not getParam('y', 2). You're doing the latter.
>
> Behind the scenes, we do map strings to numeric indexes internally. And in this case I think that is causing the behavior you are seeing. Here's an illustrative example showing the mapping in the case of `dnorm`:
>
> code <- nimbleCode({
>     y ~ dnorm(5, sd = 10)
> })
> m  <- nimbleModel(code, inits = list(y = 3))
>
> m$getParam('y', 1)  # value of y
> m$getParam('y', 2)  # mean
> m$getParam('y', 3)  # sd
> m$getParam('y', 4)  # precision
> m$getParam('y', 5)  # var
>
> [1] 3
> [1] 5
> [1] 10
> [1] 0.01
> [1] 100
>
> I think that will allow you to work through the errors/behavior you are getting.
>
> You may be able to hack something that works uncompiled using indices rather than strings as the second argument, but I haven't looked to see what will happen if you try to compile that.
>
> Happy to iterate on this.
>
> -chris

messages.body_plain:
Philip,

If you are simply trying to use nimble's functionality (in particular nimbleFunctions) in your package, then yes this is possible and there are various examples on CRAN (e.g., `BayesNSGP`, `nimbleEcology`, etc.)

But it sounds like you may want to use nimble to generate C++ and then have that as part of your package? If so then you can take that C++ and make it part of your package, either with or without using Rcpp (in the latter case, the Writing R Extensions manual has lots of (potentially hard to read) information). Using Rcpp would probably make the package creation easier --  you'd then have the internal computations use the C++ you generated via nimble, while the interfaces between R and C++ would come from Rcpp.  If you can say more about what you are trying to do, we may be able to give more guidance.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
No problem, Duoduo.  Thanks for sending the Q matrix.  First, I don't see any NA's in the response (data) value of y:

any(is.na <http://is.na>(data$y))
## [1] FALSE

And the same is true of "vec1" and "vec2" also, so I'm not entirely sure what you mean by "only consider observed response in model and skip the NA index".

That said, there's an error or two in your model code.  For one, you can't have declarations using an equal sign, like:

            add=vec1[n]
            index=vec2[add+i]

in your model code.  For deterministic model declarations, you should use the R assignment operator, "<-".

But more important, the BUGS language is declarative, not imperative, meaning each declaration (and each iteration inside a for-loop) must declare a unique node.  So this code:

    for (n in 1:1000) {
        for (i in 1:vec1[n+1]) {
            add=vec1[n]
            index=vec2[add+i]

            .....
        }}

Results in multiple declarations of "add" and "index", which you can't have.  But, we can easily take care of this by defining the equivalent constants, as:

index <- array(NA, c(1000, max(data$vec1)))

for(n in 1:1000) {
    for(i in 1:max(data$vec1)) {
        index[n,i] <- data$vec2[data$vec1[n] + i]
    }
}

(granted, this is not the most efficient way of doing this operation in R, but it's the most clear).

And then everywhere that "index" is used in these nested loops in your model code, replace it with "index[n,i]"

Also, you'll need to move "vec1" and "Q" to the constants list, and add "index" to the constants list.  Some updated code is below:

#model we fit
code=nimbleCode({
    for (n in 1:1000) {
        for (i in 1:vec1[n+1]) {

            for (k in 1:7) {

                w[n, index[n,i], k] <- pow(attribute[n, k], Q[index[n,i], k])
            }
            logit_prob[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]] <- beta[index[n,i]] + delta[index[n,i]] * prod(w[n,index[n,i], 1:7])
            prob[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]] <- exp(logit_prob[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]])

            y[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]] ~ dbern(prob[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]])
        }}
    for (n in 1:1000) {
        for (k in 1:7) {
            logit(att_prob[n, k]) <- gamma[k] * theta[n] - lambda[k]
            attribute[n, k] ~ dbern(att_prob[n, k])
        }}
    for (n in 1:1000) {theta[n]~ dnorm(0,1)}
    for (i in 1:30) {
        item_parameter[i, 1:2] ~ dmnorm(item_mu[1:2], item_den[1:2, 1:2])
        beta[i] <- item_parameter[i, 1]
        delta[i] <- item_parameter[i, 2]
    }
    for (k in 1:7) {
        lambda[k] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
        gamma[k] ~ T(dnorm(0, 1),0,)
    }
    item_mu[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    item_mu[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, 1),0,)
    R[1, 1] <- 1
    R[2, 2] <- 1
    R[1, 2] <- 0
    R[2, 1] <- 0
    item_den[1:2, 1:2] ~ dwish(R[1:2, 1:2], 2)
})

data <- list(y=y)

inits <- list(item_den = diag(2))

constants <- list(index = index, Q=Q,vec1=vec1)
model <- nimbleModel(code, data = data, inits=inits, constants = constants)

I think this will get you running, and hopefully you can move forward from here.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Keith, nice work with the rbeta4 distribution.  Overall it looks great, there's one small thing which is giving nimble trouble - which arguably should be ok, and is something I'll file an issue for us to look into.

Basically, when you define the dbeta4 density function, you specify the type of the random variable as the "x" argument, in this case a scalar value defined by "x=double(0)" in the list of arguments.  Here, when you define this, you cannot also give a default value for "x", as you had.  So the declaration needs to look like:

    run = function(x=double(0), a=double(0,default=1),b=double(0,default=1),lower=double(0,default=0),upper=double(0,default=1), log = logical(0, default = FALSE)) {

Is this a little heavy-handed of nimble's type checking?  Should default values for the "x" argument of the density function be allowed?  These are deeper questions.  But for now, changing that first line (specifically, to remove "default=0.5") should get you going.

Like I said, I'll file an issue for the development team to think more about this.

Cheers,
Daniel

Thank you for the reply, Daniel. I have changed "x=double(0,default=0.5)" to "x=double(0)". It gave a message:

Number of dimensions 1 of the return() argument does not match number 0 given in the returnType() statement. This occurred for: return((ARG5_upper_ - ARG4_lower_) * rbeta(n=ARG1_n_,shape1=ARG2_a_,shape2=ARG3_b_) + ARG4_lower_) This was part of the call: { return((ARG5_upper_ - ARG4_lower_) * rbeta(n=ARG1_n_,shape1=ARG2_a_,shape2=ARG3_b_) + ARG4_lower_)

I struggled it for a long while. I found a solution is to change rbeta4:

rbeta4 <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n = integer(0), a=double(0),b=double(0),lower=double(0),upper=double(0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    x <- (upper - lower) * rbeta(n, a, b) + lower
    return(x[1])
  })

where I must to specify "return(x[1]) " that only return a scalar to make NIMBLE work. I think this approach is awkward because rbeta4 is not vectorized. There may be a better workaround but I still am not sure how to keep rbeta4 vectorized.

messages.body_plain:
Keith, can you change the rbeta(n, a, b) inside your rbeta4 function to instead be rbeta(1, a, b)?  I should also have suggested this in my first email.

Under the hood, nimble *always* uses n=1 for calculations in the model.  I know you used the "n" argument for generating many realizations of your distribution in your script, on the line:

r = rbeta4(n=10000,a,b,lower,upper)

But the nimble compiler (type-checking) will be happier if you use "rbeta(1, a, b)" in your function code, so that it knows (always, for certain) that the return value "x" is a scalar.  Then, you should not need to say "x[1]", as you found works.

In your script, then, you will also need to change

r = rbeta4(n=10000,a,b,lower,upper)

to instead be something like:

r = replicate(10000, rbeta4(n=1,a,b,lower,upper))

Please let me know if these suggestions help.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Combine multiple individual models?
messages.subject_clean: Combine multiple individual models?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott,
Specifically what you're suggesting does not exist. We have thought about ideas like it, but they have never been created.
The nimbleCode function is essentially the same as R's native quote function.

Here is a stack function that will put together two results from nimbleCode (or quote):

stack <- function(a, b) {
   unpack <- \(x) if(x[[1]]=='{') as.list(x)[-1] else x
   as.call(c(quote(`{`), unpack(a), unpack(b)))
}

c1 <- nimbleCode({a ~ dnorm(0,1)}) # arbitrary code within {}
c2 <- nimbleCode(b ~ dexp(1)) # a single line
stack(c1, c2)

It's not as general as what you're sketching, but maybe it will give you something to compose models from pieces in a useful way.

HTH
Perry

>
>             add=vec1[n]
>             index=vec2[add+i]
>
> in your model code.  For deterministic model declarations, you should use the R assignment operator, "<-".
>
> But more important, the BUGS language is declarative, not imperative, meaning each declaration (and each iteration inside a for-loop) must declare a unique node.  So this code:
>
>     for (n in 1:1000) {
>         for (i in 1:vec1[n+1]) {
>             add=vec1[n]
>             index=vec2[add+i]
>             .....

>
>
> index <- array(NA, c(1000, max(data$vec1)))
>
> for(n in 1:1000) {
>     for(i in 1:max(data$vec1)) {
>         index[n,i] <- data$vec2[data$vec1[n] + i]
>     }
> }
>
>
> (granted, this is not the most efficient way of doing this operation in R, but it's the most clear).
>
> And then everywhere that "index" is used in these nested loops in your model code, replace it with "index[n,i]"

messages.subject_clean: Use nimblelist in nimbleCode
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am studying how to use nimblelist in nimbleCode. From the nimble documentation, it talks about how to nimblelist in nimbleFunction (p. 171), so I am not sure how to use it in nimbleCode.

I have a toy example below. The problem is the use of "T_list" ( nimblelist ) in nimbleCode:

    cal_eta_to_lambda <- nimbleFunction(
      run = function(eta=double(2), eta_loc=double(2), T_names=character(1), T=T_index_list_def() ) {
        lambda = array(0,dim(eta))
        for (i in 1:dim(eta)[2]){
          index = eta_loc[,i]
          lambda[index,i] = eta[index,i] %*% solve(T[[T_names[i]]])
        }
        returnType(double(2))
        return(lambda)
      })
    assign('cal_eta_to_lambda', cal_eta_to_lambda, envir = .GlobalEnv)

# Toy example:
    eta = matrix(0,8,16) # demo; for being able to run
    eta_loc = matrix(TRUE,8,16) # demo; for being able to run
    T_index_list <- lapply(1:16, function(i) nimbleType(name = paste0('T',i), type = 'double', dim = 2))
    T_index_list_def <- nimbleList(T_index_list)
    T_names = paste0('T', 1:itemnum)
    T = lapply(1:16, function(x) diag(8)) # demo; for being able to run
    names(T) <- T_names
    T_list <- do.call(T_index_list_def$new, T)
    cal_eta_to_lambda(eta, eta_loc, T_names, T_list)

In nimbleCode, I have the

lambda[1:8,1:16] <- cal_eta_to_lambda(eta[1:8,1:16], eta_loc[1:8,1:itemnum], T_names[1:16], T_list)

Then, R return error message:

Error in as.numeric(eval(code, constEnv)) : cannot coerce type 'S4' to vector of type 'double' In addition: Warning message: In replaceConstantsRecurse(x, constEnv, constNames) : NAs introduced by coercion

messages.subject: issues calculating WAIC
messages.subject_clean: issues calculating WAIC
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using nimble to run multistate mark-recapture models for seabirds, as I wish to estimate survival and recruitment of juvenile, immature, and adult birds, and eventually introduce environmental covariates to investigate drivers of survival and recruitment. However,  I am having issues calculating WAIC when I include 'WAIC = TRUE' in the 'nimbleMCMC' call. I get the same WAIC value of 0.000001579057 for two different models (phi, psi and p constant, and phi time-dependent, but psi and p constant). Other than this, the models give me reasonable estimates for the parameters, and appear to have converged and chains mix well. I don't understand why the WAIC isn't being calculated, as I can calculate WAIC for CJS models using single-state data.

My code is attached, and I would be very grateful for any information or advice as I am a bit of a nimble novice!

Thanks in advance,
Kirsty

messages.subject: Re: Using Compiled Nimble Functions in R packages
messages.subject_clean: Using Compiled Nimble Functions in R packages
messages.body_plain:
Hi Philip,

Unfortunately it's not something we have a good workflow for right now. It is something we're working on as part of longer-term developments.

One issue, as you point out, is that compiling nimble-generated C++ currently includes nimble .h files and links to a nimble-generated DLL or .so. In fact, the first time you call compileNimble in an R session, it first builds a DLL or .so to link against within that session. Another issue is that the R interface objects (functions and class definitions that allow you to seamlessly use the compiled results) are generated from functions within the nimble package.

I hope we can provide better tools in a refactored version of our compiler tools in the future, but sorry to say we don't have that now. I'm very glad to see your interest in the idea.

Perry

Yeah, we agree that the parallelization support is not what we would like. messages.body_plain:
Duoduo, so is it that you want to write your model, so that only the non-NA y values are used for fitting the parameters?  (and the NA values are not included in the model at all?)

If so, then you can accomplish that using a little clever indexing, which might be overall simpler than what it looks like you've done in your code with vec1, loc, try, trytry, etc.

I sketched out the main idea, but the details of the arguments to dbern(...) need to be finished:

y_NA=fread("missing_response.csv")
numNonNAs <- apply(y_NA, 1, function(x) sum(!is.na <http://is.na>(x)))
nonNAindices <- array(NA, dim(y_NA))
for(i in 1:nrow(y_NA))   nonNAindices[i,1:numNonNAs[i]] <- which(!is.na <http://is.na>(y_NA[i,]))

## include numNonNAs and nonNAindices in your constants list:
constants$numNonNAs <- numNonNAs
constants$nonNAindices <- nonNAindices

## include y_NA in your data list:
data$y_NA <- y_NA

#model we fit
code=nimbleCode({
    for (n in 1:1000) {

        ##for (i in 1:vec1[n+1]) {
        ##    add=vec1[n]
        ##    index=vec2[add+i]
        ##    for (k in 1:7) {w[n, index, k] <- pow(attribute[n, k], Q[index, k])}
        ##    logit(prob[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]]) <- beta[index] + delta[index] * prod(w[n,index, 1:7])
        ##    y[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]] ~ dbern(prob[1+(i-1)+vec1[n]])
        ##}}
        for(i in 1:numNonNAs[n]) {
            y_NA[n, nonNAindices[n,i]] ~ dbern(....)   ## you'll need to complete this

        }
    for (n in 1:1000) {
        for (k in 1:7) {
            logit(att_prob[n, k]) <- gamma[k] * theta[n] - lambda[k]
            attribute[n, k] ~ dbern(att_prob[n, k])
        }}
    for (n in 1:1000) {theta[n]~ dnorm(0,1)}
    for (i in 1:30) {
        item_parameter[i, 1:2] ~ dmnorm(item_mu[1:2], item_den[1:2, 1:2])
        beta[i] <- item_parameter[i, 1]
        delta[i] <- item_parameter[i, 2]
    }
    for (k in 1:7) {
        lambda[k] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
        gamma[k] ~ T(dnorm(0, 1),0,)
    }
    item_mu[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    item_mu[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, 1),0,)
    R[1, 1] <- 1
    R[2, 2] <- 1
    R[1, 2] <- 0
    R[2, 1] <- 0
    item_den[1:2, 1:2] ~ dwish(R[1:2, 1:2], 2)
})

I hope this helps get you started.

Cheers,
Daniel

> > But more important, the BUGS language is declarative, not imperative, meaning each declaration (and each iteration inside a for-loop) must declare a unique node.  So this code:
> >

> >

messages.subject: HMM Capture Mark Recapture with Random effects for cohorts: numerical problem with estimation
messages.subject_clean: HMM Capture Mark Recapture with Random effects for cohorts: numerical problem with estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently coding a Hidden Markov Model on Nimble. My model has two stages :

- PB: Prebreeder
- B: Breeder

One constraint is that the PB stage is 100% sure, from 1 to 5 years included. Then, from age 6, my birds can transit into the breeder stage, with a certain probability psiPB * phiPB. psiPB is the probability of reproducing as a prebreeder. PhiPB is the probability of surviving from one year to the next as a pre-Breeder. My simple model and the one with sexes as nested indexes work well.

Now I am including random effects to estimate differences in psiPB from one cohort to another. I get some weird estimations. And I do not know where it comes from.

First, Here is how I coded my random effect to estimate how the year of birth affects the psiPB parameter on a logit scale:

multistate.cate <- nimbleCode({

  # Observation matrix
  omega[1,1] <- 1-pPB
  omega[1,2] <- pPB
  omega[1,3] <- 0

  omega[2,1] <- 1-pB
  omega[2,2] <- 0
  omega[2,3] <- pB

  omega[3,1] <- 1
  omega[3,2] <- 0
  omega[3,3] <- 0

  for(i in 1:n_ind){
    for(t in (first[i]):(n_year-1)) {

      phiB[i,t] <- Mu.phiB
      phiPB[i,t] <- Mu.phiPB[age[i,t]]
      logit(psiPB[i,t]) <- logit(Mu.psiPB[age[i,t]]) + epsilon[BIRTH_YEAR[i]]

      # Transition matrix
      gamma[1,1,i,t] <- phiPB[i,t] * (1-psiPB[i,t])
      gamma[1,2,i,t] <- phiPB[i,t] * psiPB[i,t]
      gamma[1,3,i,t] <- 1-phiPB[i,t]

      gamma[2,1,i,t] <- 0
      gamma[2,2,i,t] <- phiB[i,t]
      gamma[2,3,i,t] <- 1-phiB[i,t]

      gamma[3,1,i,t] <- 0
      gamma[3,2,i,t] <- 0
      gamma[3,3,i,t] <- 1
    }
  }

  # Priors
  pPB ~ dunif(0,1)
  pB ~ dunif(0,1)
  Mu.phiB ~ dunif(0,1)

  for(a in 1:5){
    Mu.phiPB[a] ~ dunif(0,1)
    Mu.psiPB[a] ~ dunif(0,0.01)
  }

  for(a in 6:Amax){
    Mu.phiPB[a] ~ dunif(0,1)
    Mu.psiPB[a] ~ dunif(0,1)
  }

  for(birth_year in unique(BIRTH_YEAR)) {
    espilon[birth_year] ~ dnorm(0, sigma_eps)
  }
  sigma_eps ~ dunif(0, 1)

  # Likelihood
  for(i in 1:n_ind){
    # latent state at first capture
    z[i,first[i]] <- y[i,first[i]] - 1
    for(t in (first[i]+1):n_year){
      # z[i,t] given
      z[i,t] ~ dcat(gamma[z[i,t-1],1:3,i,t-1])
      y[i,t] ~ dcat(omega[z[i,t],1:3])
    }
  }

})

And the initial values that I pass to my model :

initial.values <- function(){list(phiPB = matrix(runif(ncol(y)*nrow(y), 0, 1),
                                                 ncol = ncol(y),
                                                 nrow = nrow(y)),
                                  phiB = matrix(runif(ncol(y)*nrow(y), 0, 1),
                                                ncol = ncol(y),
                                                nrow = nrow(y)),
                                  psiPB = matrix(runif(ncol(y)*nrow(y), 0, 1),
                                                 ncol = ncol(y),
                                                 nrow = nrow(y)),
                                  Mu.phiPB = c(runif(seq(1, max(age, na.rm = TRUE)), 0, 1)),
                                  Mu.psiPB = c(runif(seq(1, 5), 0, 0.001), runif(seq(6, max(age, na.rm = TRUE)), 0, 1)),
                                  Mu.phiB = 0.9,
                                  pPB = 0.8,
                                  pB = 0.9,
                                  epsilon = c(rnorm(seq(1, max(birth_year)), 0, runif(1,0,1))),
                                  sigma_eps = runif(1,0,1),
                                  z = zinits)}

Second, in the attached files, this is what I obtained for my parameters epsilon and sigma_eps. I also get the following message: NAs were detected in model variables: epsilon, logProb_espilon. This means that these parameters have problems to initialize i think.

I tried some things to figure it out what the problem is:
- Give more data and less years (so less epsilons to estimate, currently I just have 2)
- Change the prior scale and initial values for epsilon and sigma_eps.

Currently, nothing has worked. I think this is a problem of parametrization. But I need to figure out what to explore next to fix the problem and learn from my mistakes here.

Do you have a clue or something in mind that could help me to fix the problem(s) ?

Best and thank you very much for your reading. Do not hesitate if you need more input from my part.

Etienne

messages.body_plain:
We have some info about this Section 5.2.4.1.2  <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-writing-models.html#lkj-distribution-for-correlation-matrices>of the manual. That section shows what to do if you want a covariance. For a correlation, just leave out the multiplication by `sds`. As seen in the manual you should have `prec_param=0` if you are on the correlation or covariance scale (rather than the precision scale).

-chris

Announcing a new two day virtual Bayesian Disease Mapping workshop March 4-5th 2024

** A novel online access to this important event**
​*A new low student rate is also now available​*​

Using R for Bayesian Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Health Modeling
Parts I, II

March 4th - 5th 2024

COURSE CONTENT
These courses are designed to provide a comprehensive introduction to the area of Bayesian disease mapping using R in applications to Public Health and Epidemiology:  Part I will run on June 1st and Part II on June 2nd, 2023.
Part I consists of sessions dealing with:
AM
•     Basic concepts of Bayesian methods and disease mapping
•     Bayesian computation: MCMC and alternatives
PM
•     R graphics for spatial health data
•     Bayesian Hierarchical Models for disease mapping (BHMs):
Simple models:  Poisson-gamma; log-normal, convolution.
Variants: Leroux, mixture, BYM2.
•     Model goodness of fit
•     Demonstration of risk estimation and using BRugs/OpenBUGS

Part II consists of sessions dealing with
AM
•     Nimble
•     CARBayes
•     INLA
PM
•     Space-time modelling with McMC (Nimble)
•     Space-time modelling with INLA
•     Clustering in space and space-time
•     Infectious disease modelling and surveillance

THE SPEAKER
Andrew B. Lawson (Department of Public Health Sciences, College of Medicine, Medical University of South Carolina) is a MUSC Distinguished Professor Emeritus and a World Health Organization (WHO) advisor
 on Disease Mapping and organized with WHO an international workshop on this topic which has led to an edited volume “Disease Mapping and Risk Assessment for Public Health”.
He recently acted as chief editor of the CRC Handbook of Spatial Epidemiology (2016).
He has published a number of books focused on disease mapping and spatial epidemiology. In particular, the 3rd edition of the book: Lawson, A. B.  Bayesian Disease Mapping  CRC Press, appeared in 2018.

Lawson, A. B. (2023) Using R for Bayesian Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Health Modeling. CRC Press.
will be a course text for the workshop. A copy of this book is included in the fee for the in-person course. A e-book version is included in the online registration. Paperback version available at an added cost.

A variety of R packages will be used in the workshop. The main R packages used will be BRugs, Nimble, CARBayes, and INLA.

for(birth_year in unique(BIRTH_YEAR)) {

I also tried to run the model the long way by using nimbleModel(), but I got the same information.

Do you have any advice ? If I find something, I keep people updated here.

Best,
Etienne

> > > That said, there's an error or two in your model code.  For one, you can't have declarations using an equal sign, like:
> > >
> > >             add=vec1[n]
> > >             index=vec2[add+i]
> > >
> > > in your model code.  For deterministic model declarations, you should use the R assignment operator, "<-".
> > >
> > > But more important, the BUGS language is declarative, not imperative, meaning each declaration (and each iteration inside a for-loop) must declare a unique node.  So this code:
> > >
> > >     for (n in 1:1000) {
> > >         for (i in 1:vec1[n+1]) {
> > >             add=vec1[n]
> > >             index=vec2[add+i]
> > >             .....
> > >         }}

> > > Results in multiple declarations of "add" and "index", which you can't have.  But, we can easily take care of this by defining the equivalent constants, as:
> > >
> > >
> > > index <- array(NA, c(1000, max(data$vec1)))
> > >
> > > for(n in 1:1000) {
> > >     for(i in 1:max(data$vec1)) {
> > >         index[n,i] <- data$vec2[data$vec1[n] + i]
> > >     }
> > > }

> > >

messages.body_plain:
A clarification: the previous advert had conflicting dates listed for the workshop.
This is to confirm that the workshop is running on March  4th and 5th   2024.

The text below is corrected:

** A novel online access to this important event**
​*A new low student rate is also now available​*​

Using R for Bayesian Spatial and Spatio-Temporal Health Modeling
Parts I, II

March 4th - 5th 2024

COURSE CONTENT
These courses are designed to provide a comprehensive introduction to the area of Bayesian disease mapping using R in applications to Public Health and Epidemiology:  Part I will run on March 4th and Part II on March 5th 2024.
Part I consists of sessions dealing with:
AM
•     Basic concepts of Bayesian methods and disease mapping
•     Bayesian computation: MCMC and alternatives
PM
•     R graphics for spatial health data
•     Bayesian Hierarchical Models for disease mapping (BHMs):
Simple models:  Poisson-gamma; log-normal, convolution.
Variants: Leroux, mixture, BYM2.
•     Model goodness of fit
•     Demonstration of risk estimation and using BRugs/OpenBUGS

Part II consists of sessions dealing with
AM
•     Nimble
•     CARBayes
•     INLA
PM
•     Space-time modelling with McMC (Nimble)
•     Space-time modelling with INLA
•     Clustering in space and space-time
•     Infectious disease modelling and surveillance

THE SPEAKER
Andrew B. Lawson (Department of Public Health Sciences, College of Medicine, Medical University of South Carolina) is a MUSC Distinguished Professor Emeritus and a World Health Organization (WHO) advisor
 on Disease Mapping and organized with WHO an international workshop on this topic which has led to an edited volume “Disease Mapping and Risk Assessment for Public Health”.
He recently acted as chief editor of the CRC Handbook of Spatial Epidemiology (2016).
He has published a number of books focused on disease mapping and spatial epidemiology. In particular, the 3rd edition of the book: Lawson, A. B.  Bayesian Disease Mapping  CRC Press, appeared in 2018.

messages.subject_clean: coding penalized likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm attempting to code a penalized likelihood in Nimble and hitting a few stumbling blocks. I have the following model (this is the non-penalized version that is working):

X_i ~ Poisson (mu_i) (i = 1, 2, ..., 29)
mu_i = sum^{i}_{j = 1} (f(i-j)*lambda_j)
f(i-j) is defined below in the code.

I am currently using a non-informative prior for lambda_j: lambda_j~ Gamma (200000, 1). I wish to estimate lambda_i (i = 1, 2, ..., 29) via MCMC. Below is my code -- I have no issues with this code, but included for clarity. My question comes after the code. Data is attached.

#CODE----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
f <- nimbleFunction(
   run = function(x = double(1)){
     k <- 6.06
     r <- 2.94 # shape (alpha);rate (beta)

     out <- pgamma(x+1, k, rate = r) - pgamma(x, k, rate = r)
     return(out)
     returnType(double(1))
})

modelCode <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:L){
    lambda[i] ~ dgamma(alpha,beta)
    mu[i] <- sum(f(i-1:i)*lambda[1:i])
    x[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])
  }})

modelConsts <- list(L = nrow(dat),
                    alpha = mean(dat$Notifications),
                    beta = 1)
modelData <- list(x = dat$Notifications)

initsList <- list(list(lambda = abs(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean(dat$Notifications), sd(dat$Notifications)))),
                  list(lambda = abs(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean(dat$Notifications), sd(dat$Notifications)))),
                  list(lambda = abs(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean(dat$Notifications), sd(dat$Notifications)))))

model <- nimbleModel(modelCode, data = modelData, inits = initsList, constants = modelConsts)
#-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I would like to add a penalty term to my likelihood and maximize that. The desired penalty is: (1/theta)*sum^{29}_{j=3} [log(lambda_{j-2}) - 2*log(lambda_{j-1}) + log(lambda_{j}]^2. I would also like to estimate theta via MCMC, but have removed that step for simplicity for now. I've considered adding this in two ways. The first is via the distribution of X_i, i.e. giving X_i an improper distribution that incorporates in the Poisson distribution and penalty term, but I am unsure how to specify that. Changing the my model code statement to what I've posted below did not work:

modelCode <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:L){
    lambda[i] ~ dgamma(alpha,beta)
    mu[i] <- sum(f(i-1:i)*lambda[1:i])
    x[i] ~ dpois(mu[i]) - exp{-(theta/2)*sum((log(x[1:(L-2)]) - 2*log(x[2:(L-1)]) + log(x[3:L]))^2)}
  }})

I've also tried to specify my penalty as an improper prior via the following code:

dpen <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1),
                 theta = double(0), L = double(0),
                 log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- -(theta/2)*sum((log(x[1:(L-2)]) - 2*log(x[2:(L-1)]) + log(x[3:L]))^2)
    if(log) return(logProb)
    else return(exp(logProb))
  })
modelCode <- nimbleCode({

  for (i in 1:L){
    #get mu
    mu[i] <- sum(f(i-1:i)*lambda[1:i])

    #likelihood
    x[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])}

  lambda[1:L] ~ dpen(theta = theta, L = L)
  })

modelConsts <- list(L = nrow(dat),
                    theta = .1)
modelData <- list(x = dat$Notifications)

initsList <- list(lambda = abs(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean(dat$Notifications), sd(dat$Notifications))))

model <- nimbleModel(modelCode, data = modelData, inits = initsList, constants = modelConsts)

Running the nimbleModel line gives the following error: Defining model
Error in if (currentVertexCounts[VID] != numWithinBlock) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

Any suggestions in defining this penalized likelihood MCMC problem would be greatly appreciated. Please let me know if I can provide any additional information.

Thanks,
Annie

messages.subject: No conjugacy in augmented probit latent space network model (and likely other issues)
messages.subject_clean: No conjugacy in augmented probit latent space network model (and likely other issues)
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm very new to NIMBLE and I suspect there may be many errors in my approach, so apologies in advance.

I'm attempting to fit a simple inner product network model in the style of Hoff and Raftery (2002). My standard approach would be to use a Gibbs sampler for Polya-gamma data augmented logistic regression, but I found that the Polya-gamma is not in NIMBLE's distribution library so conjugacy is not detected. Instead I'm attempting probit data augmentation instead, but I'm still seeing that conjugacy is not detected and I'm getting an "Infinite values were detected in model variable: logProb_Y" error for all edges (Y_ij ==1). Alternatively, using nimbleHMC (and dropping the data augmentation), I get reasonable recovery, so it seems I'm not specifying the data augmentation scheme correctly in my Nimble model, and I would like to get the conjugate sampler working if possible.

My code is below.

Thanks,

Jennifer

#---------------------------------------------- SIMULATE DATA -----------------------------------------#

# Simulate data from an inner product network model
set.seed(1234)

# Data (and latent space) structure
V <- 100 # Number of vertices
H <- 10 # Dimension of latent space

# Hyperparameters
a1 <- 2.5 # Gamma shrinkage parameter for factor 1
a2 <- 2.5 # Gamma shrinkage parameters for factors 2:H
sd.e <- 0.1 # Gaussian noise added to linear predictor
meanP <- 0.25 # Moderately sparse network
mu0 <- probit(meanP) # Prior mean for intercept
sd.mu <http://sd.mu> <- 0.1 # Prior sd for intercept: consider probit scale

# Simulate multiplicative gamma shrinkage process
U <- rep(NA,H)
U[1] <- rgamma(1, a1, 1)
U[2:H] <- rgamma(H-1, a2, 1)

Tau <- rep(NA, H)
for(h in 1:H){
  Tau[h] <- prod(U[1:h])
}

# Simulate latent factors
X <- matrix(NA, nrow = V, ncol = H)
for(h in 1:H){
  X[,h] <- rmvnorm(n = 1, mean = rep(0, V), sigma = diag(Tau[h]^(-1), nrow = V))
}

# Simulate intercept
mu <- rnorm(1,mean = mu0, sd = sd.mu <http://sd.mu>) # Normal prior for baseline connection score

# Compute the linear predictor and Z latent connection score
M.Z <- mu + X %*% t(X)
vecE <- rnorm(V*(V-1)/2, 0, sd.e)
E <- matrix(NA, V,V)
E[upper.tri(E)] <- vecE
E[lower.tri(E)] <- t(E)[lower.tri(E)]
diag(E) <- 0
Z <- M.Z + E # Data augmentation approach

# Simulate edges and non-edges
Y <- ifelse(Z > 0, 1, 0)
diag(Y) <- diag(Z) <- 0 # No self-edges

#----------------------------------------- DEFINE NIMBLE MODEL---------------------------------------------#
fmCode <- nimbleCode({

  # Intercept
  mu ~ dnorm(mu0, sd = sd.mu <http://sd.mu>)

  # Shrinkage process
  U[1] ~ dgamma(a1, 1)
  for(h in 2:H){
    U[h] ~ dgamma(a2, 1)
  }

  for(h in 1:H){
    Tau[h] <- prod(U[1:h])
  }

  # Latent factors
  for(h in 1:H){
    for(v in 1:V){
      X[v,h] ~ dnorm(M[v] , sd = sqrt(Tau[h]^(-1)))
    }
  }

  # Compute linear predictor
  M.Z[1:V,1:V] <- mu + X[,] %*% t(X[,]) # Recall multivariate nodes must be used with []

  # Model
  for (i in 2:V){
    for (j in 1:(i-1)){ # Self-edges not allowed
      E[i,j] ~ dnorm(mean = 0, sd = sd.e)
      Z[i,j] <- M.Z[i,j] + E[i,j]
      indZ[i,j] <- getIndicator(Z[i,j]) # Function required to pass indices to if statement
      Y[i,j] ~ dbin(size = 1, prob = indZ[i,j])
    }
  }

})

# Function to get indicator
getIndicator <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(Zij = double(0)) {
    if(Zij > 0){
      Yij <- 1
    }else{
      Yij <- 0
    }
    return(Yij)
    returnType(double(0))
  })

# Define the constants
mu0 = probit(mean(Y, na.rm = TRUE)) # Reasonable guess for intercept prior mean

fmConsts <- list(V = V,
                 H = H,
                  a1 = a1, a2 = a2,
                  mu0 = mu0, sd.mu <http://sd.mu> = sd.mu <http://sd.mu>,
                  M = rep(0, V), sd.e = sd.e)

# Define the data
fmData <- list(Y = Y)

# Set initialization parameters
fmInits <- list(X = matrix(0, V, H),
                U = 1:H,
                mu = mu0,
                E = matrix(0,V,V),
                Z = ifelse(Y==1, 1, -1),
                indZ = Y)

fmDims <- list(Tau = H, X = c(V, H), mvCov = c(V,V,H),
              E = c(V,V))

# Create NIMBLE model
fm <- nimbleModel(code = fmCode, name = "fm", constants = fmConsts, data = fmData,
                   dimensions = fmDims, inits = fmInits)

# Check conjugacy
configureMCMC(fm, print = TRUE) # no conjugacy

# ------------------------------------ FIT MODEL AND EVALUATE----------------------------------------#
niter <- 2000
nchains <- 2
mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code = fmCode, constants = fmConsts,
                       data = fmData, inits = fmInits,
                       nchains = nchains, niter = niter,
                       summary = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE,
                       monitors = c('mu', 'Z', 'Tau'))

# Check recovery of latent probabilities
fm.samples <- do.call(rbind, mcmc.out$samples)
p.samples <- fm.samples[, grepl("P", colnames(fm.samples))]

p.post <http://p.post> <- matrix(data = colMeans(p.samples), byrow = FALSE, nrow = V, ncol = V)
diag(p.post <http://p.post>) <- 0
plot(c(p.post <http://p.post>), c(P))

messages.subject: Re: issues calculating WAIC
messages.subject_clean: issues calculating WAIC
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kirsty (following on some off-list discussion),

The problem here is that the likelihood is not changing as the parameters change. The reason is that the way the model
is defined, `z[i,t]` says which row of `omega` is used for `y[i,t]`. As the MCMC proceeds, a given `z[i,t]` can only
be such that the observed `y[i,t]` is possible, and the probability vector for the `dcat` for `y` has a probability of one
in one position and zero in the others. So the probability density for y is always 1 (log probability density always 0) for
every MCMC iteration (i.e., regardless of the current parameter values) since values of z that don't make this be the case
would be rejected.

I started to think about the marginal version of WAIC, averaging over possible `z` values, but if one simulates `z` values
based on current parameter values in the MCMC but not conditioning on the data (as would happen with marginal WAIC),
one will produce `z` values that cause the likelihood to be 0. So I don't think that will work.
So ultimately, I think there's a statistical question in terms of how to apply  WAIC to this model structure, not a nimble issue.

Also, this is perhaps a side note but perhaps relevant --  I'm not understanding how the model can give a valid (non-zero) likelihood for the y's that
are equal to 2. None of the rows of `omega` have positive probability on the second element. I must not be seeing/understanding
something.

As you may have noticed, the value of `pWAIC` that nimble is returning is 0 and the value of `lppd` is essentially zero
(seemingly up to some floating point numerical imprecision). This reflects the issue above and is the reason you get the same
"WAIC" for both models.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Dear Etienne,

I see a few things that might be going on that I can speculate about.

The first is that for(birth_year in unique(BIRTH_YEAR)) is not supported in model code. Only sequential indices can be used. So you would need something like:
for(i in 1:num_birth_years) {
espilon[unique_birth_year[i]] ~ dnorm(0, sigma_eps)
}
where you would create
unique_birth_year <- unique(BIRTH_YEAR)
num_birth_years <- length(unique_birth_year)
 in R and provide them in the constants list.

The second is that you might be assuming some variables are visible (in scope) when the initial.values function is called that might not necessarily be in scope. For example, ncol(y) depends on having y in scope, max(birth_year) depends on having birth_year in scope, etc. Maybe they are. I just can't tell. Even worse, the function might be seeing values of those variables using R's lexical scoping that are in (e.g.) the R global environment and could even be different from the ones you have in the data and/or constants lists.

The third is that

 logit(psiPB[i,t]) <- logit(Mu.psiPB[age[i,t]]) + epsilon[BIRTH_YEAR[i]]

can potentially result in NA if Mu.psiPB[age[i,t]] happens to be too close to 0 or epsilon[BIRTH_YEAR[i]] happens to be invalid.

My guess is that the invalid for() construction is causing multiple of these problems.

HTH
Perry

Now that I have my model running, I actually have another question about hyperpriors. I specify my model as follows, with the desire for theta to have a hyperprior of Unif(0, 100). However, the code only estimates theta, whereas I would like it to estimate theta and all lambdas. Would you be able to explain what is happening/how to fix? Thanks again!

f_vec <- nimbleFunction(
   run = function(x = double(0)){

     k <- 6.06 # shape
     r <- 1/.34 # scale = 1/rate

     tmp_vec <- rep(NA, x)

     for (i in 1:x) {
       tmp_vec[i] <- pgamma(x-(i-1), k, rate = r) - pgamma(x-i, k, rate = r)
     }

     return(tmp_vec)
     returnType(double(1))
})

dpen <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1),
                 theta = double(0), L = double(0),
                 log = integer(0, default = 0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    logProb <- -(theta/2)*sum((log(x[1:(L-2)]) - 2*log(x[2:(L-1)]) + log(x[3:L]))^2)
    if(log) return(logProb)
    else return(exp(logProb))
  })

modelCode <- nimbleCode({

  for (i in 1:L){
    #get mu

    mu[i] <- sum(f_vec(i)*lambda[1:i])

    #likelihood
    x[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])}

  lambda[1:L] ~ dpen(theta = theta, L = L)

  theta ~ dunif(1, 100)
  })

modelConsts <- list(L = nrow(dat))

modelData <- list(x = dat$Notifications)

model <- nimbleModel(modelCode, data = modelData, constants = modelConsts)

# compile into nimble
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)

#run MCMC
modelConf <- configureMCMC(Cmodel, enableWAIC = TRUE)
modelMCMC <- buildMCMC(modelConf)
CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(modelMCMC)

niter <- 20000
initsList <- list(list(lambda = abs(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean(dat$Notifications), sd(dat$Notifications))),
                       theta = runif(1, 0, 100)),
                  list(lambda = abs(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean(dat$Notifications), sd(dat$Notifications))),
                       theta = runif(1, 0, 100)),
                  list(lambda = abs(rnorm(nrow(dat), mean(dat$Notifications), sd(dat$Notifications))),
                       theta = runif(1, 0, 100)))

mcmc.out <- runMCMC(CmodelMCMC, inits = initsList,
                    niter = niter, nchains = 3, nburnin = 10000, thin = 10,
                    summary = T, WAIC = T)

Hi, Dan. I tried the method you mentioned to run the model. It can get the MCMC result with no error. However, the estimated parameter is very different than the true parameter I set. In my opinion, the method that directly see the missing response as latent variable is similar to the method that skip the index of missing response(we did right now, only consider observed response in the MCMC). I give the code and data below and I am not sure if I made any mistake here. Do you have any idea about this? Thanks!

library(scales)

library(nimble)

set.seed(1994)

theta=c()

}

lamda=c(-1.5,-1,-0.5,0,0.5,1,1.5)

parameter_DINA_alpha_lamda<-cbind(alpha,lamda)
parameter_DINA_beta_zeta<-beta_zeta
colnames(parameter_DINA_beta_zeta) <- c('beta','zeta')
parameter_DINA_theta<-as.data.frame(theta)
parameter_DINA_alpha_lamda<-as.data.frame(parameter_DINA_alpha_lamda)

lamdaD<-lamda
thetaD<-theta
betaD<-parameter_DINA_beta_zeta$beta
zetaD<-parameter_DINA_beta_zeta$zeta
gammaD<-alpha

Q=data.frame(matrix(ncol = 7,nrow = 30))

#good method

for(i in 1:nrow(y))   nonNAindices[i,1:numNonNAs[i]] <- which(!is.na <http://is.na>(y[i,]))

#model we fit
code=nimbleCode({
  for (n in 1:1000) {

    for(i in 1:numNonNAs[n]) {

      for (k in 1:7) {w[n, nonNAindices[n,i], k] <- pow(attribute[n, k], Q[nonNAindices[n,i], k])}
      logit(prob[n, nonNAindices[n,i]]) <- beta[nonNAindices[n,i]] + delta[nonNAindices[n,i]] * prod(w[n, nonNAindices[n,i], 1:7])
      y[n, nonNAindices[n,i]] ~ dbern(prob[n, nonNAindices[n,i]])   ## you'll need to complete this

    }}
  for (n in 1:1000) {
    for (k in 1:7) {
      logit(att_prob[n, k]) <- gamma[k] * theta[n] - lambda[k]
      attribute[n, k] ~ dbern(att_prob[n, k])
    }}
  for (n in 1:1000) {theta[n]~ dnorm(0,1)}
  for (i in 1:30) {
    item_parameter[i, 1:2] ~ dmnorm(item_mu[1:2], item_den[1:2, 1:2])
    beta[i] <- item_parameter[i, 1]
    delta[i] <- item_parameter[i, 2]
  }
  for (k in 1:7) {
    lambda[k] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
    gamma[k] ~ T(dnorm(0, 1),0,)
  }
  item_mu[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  item_mu[2] ~ T(dnorm(0, 1),0,)
  R[1, 1] <- 1
  R[2, 2] <- 1
  R[1, 2] <- 0
  R[2, 1] <- 0
  item_den[1:2, 1:2] ~ dwish(R[1:2, 1:2], 2)
})

data <- list(y=y,Q=Q)

inits <- list(item_den = diag(2))

Consts <- list(numNonNAs = numNonNAs,
               nonNAindices=nonNAindices)

monitors=c("gamma","lambda","beta","delta")

model<-nimbleModel(code,data = data,inits=inits,constants = Consts)

cModel_DINA <-compileNimble(model)
conf_DINA <- configureMCMC(model, monitors = monitors)
model_DINAMCMC <- buildMCMC(conf_DINA)
cModel_DINAMCMC <- compileNimble(model_DINAMCMC, project = model)
system.time(samples_DINA<-runMCMC(cModel_DINAMCMC,

                                  nchains=2,niter = 80000, nburnin = 10000))

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jennifer, a few comments here.

1) For a basic probit data augmentation, you could write something like this:

```
y[i,j] ~ dinterval(z[i,j], 0)
z[i,j] ~ dnorm(beta0 + beta1*x[i,j], 1)
beta0 ~ dnorm(0,1)
beta1 ~ dnorm(0,1)
```
and conjugacy should be detected in nimble for sampling the beta parameters.  `dinterval` is basically a trick to enforce that z[i,j] > 0 if y[i,j] = 1 and z[i,j] <= 0 if y[i,j] = 0. (One could also use `dconstraint`.) See Section 5.2.7 of the manual for more details on `dinterval` and `dconstraint`.

2) Without delving into Hoff and Raftery and thinking more carefully about the model, I don't have specific things to suggest in terms of writing your model, but hopefully the above code will help get you started.
I'm happy to iterate here if you have follow-up questions or can say more about which parameters you're expecting to be sampled based on conjugacy. (I'm actually not seeing what you're expecting
to be conjugate.)

3) We may do some work in coming weeks to make a Polya-gamma sampler available (initially in our development branch). I don't want to promise anything, but it's something we've wanted
to set up for a while and have some other projects going on that could make use of it. I can try to remember to let you know if/when we make progress on that.

4) As far as the logProb_y infinity situation, I'm not immediately seeing what might cause that. One common issue in situations like this is setting incompatible data/initial values for `Y[i,j]` and `Z[i,j]` pairs such that the log density is `-Inf`, but you indicated the message is about getting `Inf`. Despite that, it may relate to model initialization - we have some tips on that here in the manual <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-mcmc.html#sec:initMCMC>.

-chris

>

>

Hi Chris,

Thanks so much. To simplify things, I'm starting with a more basic network regression. I attempted the probit data augmentation approach using your suggested construction of Y,Z with a simple network probit regression, and Nimble does now detect conjugacy (although not for z, which should have truncated normal full conditional), and giving marginal improvement on the RW sampler .

However, when I add random effects, I can fit it using the RW sampler, but using the conjugate sampler I'm getting the following error:  warning: logProb of data node y[26, 14]: logProb is -Inf.

Do you have any suggestions what could be causing the issue? My code is below and I'm happy to share the data via email if there's no obvious error.

## define the model
glmmCode2 <- nimbleCode({

  #beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1) # Drop intercept
  beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
  sigma_RE ~ dunif(0, 10)

  # Model
  for(i in 1:N){ # Random effects for each vertex
    beta2[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma_RE)
  }
  for (i in 2:N) { # Likelihood

    for (j in 1:(i-1)){

      y[i,j] ~ dinterval(z[i,j], 0)

      z[i,j] ~ dnorm(beta1*x[i,j] + beta2[i] + beta2[j], 1)
    }
  }
})

## constants, data, and initial values
glmmConsts2 <- list(N = nC)

glmmData2 <- list(
  y = A,
  x = outer(reg,reg, FUN = "==")*1 # x_ij = 1(region_i == region_j)
)

glmmInits2 <- list(beta1 = 0, beta2 = rep(0,nC))

glmmModel2 <- nimbleModel(code = glmmCode2, constants = glmmConsts2, data = glmmData2,
                         inits = glmmInits2)

configureMCMC(glmmModel2, print = TRUE)

niter <- 2000
nchains <- 2

mcmc.glmm.out2 <- nimbleMCMC(code = glmmCode2, constants = glmmConsts2,
                       data = glmmData2, inits = glmmInits2,

                       nchains = nchains, niter = niter,
                       summary = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE,

                       monitors = c('beta1', 'beta2'))

Best,

Jennifer

> > diag(E) <- 0
> > Z <- M.Z + E # Data augmentation approach
> >
> > # Simulate edges and non-edges
> > Y <- ifelse(Z > 0, 1, 0)
> > diag(Y) <- diag(Z) <- 0 # No self-edges
> >
> > #----------------------------------------- DEFINE NIMBLE MODEL---------------------------------------------#
> > fmCode <- nimbleCode({
> >
> >   # Intercept
> >   mu ~ dnorm(mu0, sd = sd.mu <http://sd.mu>)
> >
> >   # Shrinkage process
> >   U[1] ~ dgamma(a1, 1)
> >   for(h in 2:H){
> >     U[h] ~ dgamma(a2, 1)
> >   }
> >
> >   for(h in 1:H){
> >     Tau[h] <- prod(U[1:h])
> >   }
> >
> >   # Latent factors
> >   for(h in 1:H){
> >     for(v in 1:V){
> >       X[v,h] ~ dnorm(M[v] , sd = sqrt(Tau[h]^(-1)))
> >     }
> >   }
> >
> >   # Compute linear predictor
> >   M.Z[1:V,1:V] <- mu + X[,] %*% t(X[,]) # Recall multivariate nodes must be used with []
> >
> >   # Model
> >   for (i in 2:V){
> >     for (j in 1:(i-1)){ # Self-edges not allowed
> >       E[i,j] ~ dnorm(mean = 0, sd = sd.e)
> >       Z[i,j] <- M.Z[i,j] + E[i,j]
> >       indZ[i,j] <- getIndicator(Z[i,j]) # Function required to pass indices to if statement
> >       Y[i,j] ~ dbin(size = 1, prob = indZ[i,j])
> >     }
> >   }
> >
> > })
> >
> >
> > # Function to get indicator
> > getIndicator <- nimbleFunction(
> >   run = function(Zij = double(0)) {
> >     if(Zij > 0){
> >       Yij <- 1
> >     }else{
> >       Yij <- 0
> >     }
> >     return(Yij)
> >     returnType(double(0))
> >   })
> >
> >
> > # Define the constants
> > mu0 = probit(mean(Y, na.rm = TRUE)) # Reasonable guess for intercept prior mean
> >
> > fmConsts <- list(V = V,
> >                  H = H,
> >                   a1 = a1, a2 = a2,
> >                   mu0 = mu0, sd.mu <http://sd.mu> = sd.mu <http://sd.mu>,
> >                   M = rep(0, V), sd.e = sd.e)
> >
> > # Define the data
> > fmData <- list(Y = Y)
> >
> > # Set initialization parameters
> > fmInits <- list(X = matrix(0, V, H),
> >                 U = 1:H,
> >                 mu = mu0,
> >                 E = matrix(0,V,V),
> >                 Z = ifelse(Y==1, 1, -1),
> >                 indZ = Y)
> >
> > fmDims <- list(Tau = H, X = c(V, H), mvCov = c(V,V,H),
> >               E = c(V,V))
> >
> > # Create NIMBLE model
> > fm <- nimbleModel(code = fmCode, name = "fm", constants = fmConsts, data = fmData,
> >                    dimensions = fmDims, inits = fmInits)
> >
> > # Check conjugacy
> > configureMCMC(fm, print = TRUE) # no conjugacy
> >
> > # ------------------------------------ FIT MODEL AND EVALUATE----------------------------------------#
> > niter <- 2000
> > nchains <- 2
> > mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code = fmCode, constants = fmConsts,
> >                        data = fmData, inits = fmInits,
> >                        nchains = nchains, niter = niter,
> >                        summary = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE,
> >                        monitors = c('mu', 'Z', 'Tau'))
> >
> > # Check recovery of latent probabilities
> > fm.samples <- do.call(rbind, mcmc.out$samples)
> > p.samples <- fm.samples[, grepl("P", colnames(fm.samples))]
> >
> > p.post <http://p.post> <- matrix(data = colMeans(p.samples), byrow = FALSE, nrow = V, ncol = V)
> > diag(p.post <http://p.post>) <- 0
> > plot(c(p.post <http://p.post>), c(P))
> >
> >
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jennifer,

Regarding the truncated normal, we don't have that conjugacy set up. However, if you wanted to put in a bit of time, you could code up a user-defined sampler <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-progr-with-models.html#sec:user-samplers> to do the job, presuming using the inverse CDF method.
That said, I suspect that in many cases the lack of a conjugate sampler for those parameters would not be the main contributor to mixing issues.

As far as the -Inf, I suspect it is because you are not explicitly initializing the `z` values. You should initialize them such that they are consistent with the `y` values. I suspect that the initial value of `z[26,14]` is not consistent with its corresponding 'y[26,14]`.

-chris

> Hi Chris,
>
> Thanks so much. To simplify things, I'm starting with a more basic network regression. I attempted the probit data augmentation approach using your suggested construction of Y,Z with a simple network probit regression, and Nimble does now detect conjugacy (although not for z, which should have truncated normal full conditional), and giving marginal improvement on the RW sampler .
>
> However, when I add random effects, I can fit it using the RW sampler, but using the conjugate sampler I'm getting the following error:  warning: logProb of data node y[26, 14]: logProb is -Inf.
>
> Do you have any suggestions what could be causing the issue? My code is below and I'm happy to share the data via email if there's no obvious error.
>
>
> ## define the model
> glmmCode2 <- nimbleCode({
>
>   #beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1) # Drop intercept
>   beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 1)
>   sigma_RE ~ dunif(0, 10)
>
>   # Model
>   for(i in 1:N){ # Random effects for each vertex
>     beta2[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma_RE)
>   }
>   for (i in 2:N) { # Likelihood
>     for (j in 1:(i-1)){
>       y[i,j] ~ dinterval(z[i,j], 0)
>       z[i,j] ~ dnorm(beta1*x[i,j] + beta2[i] + beta2[j], 1)
>     }
>   }
> })
>
>
> ## constants, data, and initial values
> glmmConsts2 <- list(N = nC)
>
> glmmData2 <- list(
>   y = A,
>   x = outer(reg,reg, FUN = "==")*1 # x_ij = 1(region_i == region_j)
> )
>
> glmmInits2 <- list(beta1 = 0, beta2 = rep(0,nC))
>
> glmmModel2 <- nimbleModel(code = glmmCode2, constants = glmmConsts2, data = glmmData2,
>                          inits = glmmInits2)
>
> configureMCMC(glmmModel2, print = TRUE)
>
> niter <- 2000
> nchains <- 2
> mcmc.glmm.out2 <- nimbleMCMC(code = glmmCode2, constants = glmmConsts2,
>                        data = glmmData2, inits = glmmInits2,
>                        nchains = nchains, niter = niter,

>                        monitors = c('beta1', 'beta2'))
>
> Best,
>
> Jennifer
>
> On Monday, October 23, 2023 at 9:22:38 PM UTC-4 Chris Paciorek wrote:
> > Hi Jennifer, a few comments here.
> >
> > 1) For a basic probit data augmentation, you could write something like this:
> >
> > ```
> > y[i,j] ~ dinterval(z[i,j], 0)
> > z[i,j] ~ dnorm(beta0 + beta1*x[i,j], 1)
> > beta0 ~ dnorm(0,1)
> > beta1 ~ dnorm(0,1)

To follow up on Wei's point, if you wrote the `rsmooth` function to generate from your "smooth" distribution, it would return a vector, but the density function returns the joint density (which is a scalar) of the vector-valued random variable.

> > > >       Yij <- 0

> > > >   })
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > # Define the constants
> > > > mu0 = probit(mean(Y, na.rm = TRUE)) # Reasonable guess for intercept prior mean

> > > > fmConsts <- list(V = V,
> > > >                  H = H,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jennifer, this issue just came up in this user post <https://groups.google.com/g/nimble-users/c/HJV59YtS-w4>.  That was a different model but the same structure in that the data are simply imposing a constraint on some latent variables. Our WAIC calculates the likelihood of the data, which in this case are enforced to always have probability of 1 (log-prob of 0, hence what you are seeing for WAIC). So I don't know of a way to get WAIC for the data augmentation formulation of the model.

I don't know if anyone has written anything in the literature about WAIC in data augmentation contexts like this.

You mentioned fitting with nimbleHMC (i.e., without data augmentation) so you might consider using that model formulation either with nimbleHMC or some other sampling scheme. You should be able to get WAIC from that.

-chris

On Wed, Oct 25, 2023 at 4:49 PM Jennifer Kampe <jennif...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Chris,
>
> Thanks, it was indeed the initialization for Z - I had it in my simple sampler than left it out in the random effects version somehow. The model now runs, but the data augmentation scheme seems to be causing implausible values in the WAIC (WAIC \approx 0), what is to work around this?
>
> Thanks,
>
> Jennifer
>
> On Tuesday, October 24, 2023 at 8:33:27 PM UTC-4 Chris Paciorek wrote:
> > Hi Jennifer,
> >
> > Regarding the truncated normal, we don't have that conjugacy set up. However, if you wanted to put in a bit of time, you could code up a user-defined sampler <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-progr-with-models.html#sec:user-samplers> to do the job, presuming using the inverse CDF method.
> > That said, I suspect that in many cases the lack of a conjugate sampler for those parameters would not be the main contributor to mixing issues.
> >
> > As far as the -Inf, I suspect it is because you are not explicitly initializing the `z` values. You should initialize them such that they are consistent with the `y` values. I suspect that the initial value of `z[26,14]` is not consistent with its corresponding 'y[26,14]`.
> >
> > -chris
> >
> > On Tue, Oct 24, 2023 at 8:14 AM Jennifer Kampe <jennif...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi Chris,
> > >
> > > Thanks so much. To simplify things, I'm starting with a more basic network regression. I attempted the probit data augmentation approach using your suggested construction of Y,Z with a simple network probit regression, and Nimble does now detect conjugacy (although not for z, which should have truncated normal full conditional), and giving marginal improvement on the RW sampler .

> > >       y[i,j] ~ dinterval(z[i,j], 0)

> > >     }
> > >   }
> > > })
> > >
> > >

> > > > Hi Jennifer, a few comments here.

> > > > 1) For a basic probit data augmentation, you could write something like this:
> > > >
> > > > ```
> > > > y[i,j] ~ dinterval(z[i,j], 0)

> > > > beta0 ~ dnorm(0,1)
> > > > beta1 ~ dnorm(0,1)
> > > > ```
> > > > and conjugacy should be detected in nimble for sampling the beta parameters.  `dinterval` is basically a trick to enforce that z[i,j] > 0 if y[i,j] = 1 and z[i,j] <= 0 if y[i,j] = 0. (One could also use `dconstraint`.) See Section 5.2.7 of the manual for more details on `dinterval` and `dconstraint`.

messages.body_plain:
So, one issue that I was having with creating packages for my nimble functions is that they wanted to compile at *load* time.  This is not good if I have lots of nimble functions, and users only need one.

To help with this, I created this:

```
memoiseNimbleCompilation <- function(nimbleF) {
  # not sure why we need this, but nimble complains otherwise
  nimbleF <- nimbleF
  compiledFunction <- NULL
  maybeCompiledFunction <- function(...) {
    if (is.null(compiledFunction)) {
      compiledFunction <<- compileNimble(nimbleF)
    }
    return(compiledFunction(...))
  }
  return(maybeCompiledFunction)
}
```

You can use it like this:

`theCompiledFunction <- memoiseNimbleCompilation(theUncompiledFunction)`

This makes it so that compilation is "lazy", and gets deferred until the moment a user attempts to call the function.  Of course, this only works for nimble functions, but I suppose a similar thing could be arranged for models, or mcmc builds or what have you.

Hey Jennifer,
I've written a basic polya-gamma sampler for this type of problem. I wrote it today and you'll be the first to use it so please let me know if it falls apart. It was on my to do list so this thread was a good excuse. The LogisticRegression.R file is the basic example and samplePolyaGamma.R has all the Nimble code to run it. I take no responsibility for it yet but if you use it please give us some feedback. It will only currently work for dnorm fixed and random effects, not multivariate normal yet. You'll need to pass the sampler the design matrix, the size of ~dbin and the name of the response variable that is ~dbin. If it's all bernoulli you can just put size = 1.

Paul

messages.body_plain:
Hey Bert,
I ran into this same issue for a problem I'm working on. One solution is to trick the compiler to define the parameter names in advance using nimble virtual functions.

I wrote these two functions below. You can adapt them as you like.

getParam_BASE <- nimbleFunctionVirtual(
  run = function() {},
  methods = list(
getMean = function(){returnType(double(1))},
getPrecision = function(){returnType(double(2))},
getBlockIndices = function(){returnType(double(1))},
getGauss = function(){returnType(integer(0))}
)
)

buildGaussianParameters <- nimbleFunction(
  contains = getParam_BASE,
  setup = function(model, nodeName, index, nparams) {
distrNames <- c("dnorm", "dmnorm")
distr <- model$getDistribution(nodeName)
precName = "prec"
if(distr == "dnorm") precName <- "tau"
gauss <- 0
if(distr %in% distrNames) gauss <- 1
},
run = function(){},
methods = list(
getMean = function(){
returnType(double(1))
mu <- numeric(model$getParam(nodeName, "mean"), length = nparams)
return(mu)
},
getPrecision = function(){
Q <- matrix(model$getParam(nodeName, precName), nrow = nparams, ncol = nparams)
returnType(double(2))
return(Q)
},
getBlockIndices = function(){
ind <- index:(index+nparams-1)
returnType(double(1))
return(ind)
},
getGauss = function(){
returnType(integer())
return(gauss)
}
)
)

In my setup code I then built the nimble function list as follows for what I needed.
    gaussNode_nfl <- nimbleFunctionList(getParam_BASE)
for( i in 1:nreNodes ){
gaussNode_nfl[[i]] <- buildGaussianParameters(model, randomEffectsNodes[i], i, 1)
}

Within run or methods you can then call the list and access the different parameters. You can ignore a lot of this for my own specific problem. Let me know if this isn't obvious for your purposes.

e.g., in run()
Q <- gaussNode_nfl[[1]]$getPrecision()

will give me precision for the first node.

Cheers,
Paul

> On Sat, Oct 7, 2023 at 12:10 PM Chris Paciorek <paci...@stat.berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > Hi Bert,
> >
> > `getParam` is designed to work with the second arg being the character string name of a parameter, not a position in the set of arguments,
> > i.e., getParam('y', 'var') not getParam('y', 2). You're doing the latter.
> >
> > Behind the scenes, we do map strings to numeric indexes internally. And in this case I think that is causing the behavior you are seeing. Here's an illustrative example showing the mapping in the case of `dnorm`:
> >
> > code <- nimbleCode({
> >     y ~ dnorm(5, sd = 10)
> > })
> > m  <- nimbleModel(code, inits = list(y = 3))
> >
> > m$getParam('y', 1)  # value of y
> > m$getParam('y', 2)  # mean
> > m$getParam('y', 3)  # sd
> > m$getParam('y', 4)  # precision
> > m$getParam('y', 5)  # var
> >
> > [1] 3
> > [1] 5
> > [1] 10
> > [1] 0.01
> > [1] 100
> >
> > I think that will allow you to work through the errors/behavior you are getting.
> >
> > You may be able to hack something that works uncompiled using indices rather than strings as the second argument, but I haven't looked to see what will happen if you try to compile that.
> >
> > Happy to iterate on this.
> >
> > -chris

> > >

To do so, I check if a prior has a normal or multivariate normal distribution, and retrieve the appropriate hyperparameter by either itsr index slot.
> > >
> > > So, in the "setup" code I check each parameter its distribution, and store the index of the appropriate hyperparameter slot in an integer vector. When accessing the "run" code in the model directly this works fine, but when compiling the sampler I run into issues.
> > >
> > > Attached a minimum reproducible example, I am grateful for any suggestions on what I might be doing wrong here, and suggestions on how to approach this issue instead.

messages.body_plain:
Dear NIMBLE developers,

I ran into a question about the behavior of the "is.na <http://is.na>" function on p.135 of the documentation:

library("nimble")

is_na <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = double(1)) {
    if (is.na <http://is.na>(x)){
      print(x)
    }
    returnType(double(1))
    return(x)
  })
assign('is_na', is_na, envir = .GlobalEnv)
is_na_c = compileNimble(is_na)
x = c(NA,1,1)
is_na_c(x)
is_na(x)

The uncompiled version cannot run it because " Error in if (is.na <http://is.na>(x)) { : the condition has length > 1 ". When compiling it by nimbleModel(), it also returned this error but continued to proceed.

In the compiled version, it seems that the is.na <http://is.na>() accepts a vector and returns a scalar. I think its behavior is different from the is.na <http://is.na>() in base R.

I wonder:
1. How to avoid the error above when compiling it by nimbleModel(). Just ignore it?
2. What is the correct way to use is.na <http://is.na>() in the nimbleFunction?

Thanks a lot!
Keith

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luca,

A couple thoughts on how to investigate further:

1) Check the posterior for `r` -- does it collapse to putting all its mass on one element?

2) If not, try to see whether other values of Z[i] are reasonable for a given i. In particular, consider one of the Z[i]'s that is always equal to one in the MCMC. After running the MCMC for a bit,  try changing that Z[i] to the various other possible values in the compiled model and see what the result of compiled_model$calculate() is.  Possibly for some reason, all the other values give terrible model log probability values. If so try to see what part of the model is preventing Z[i] from being some other value. Note that by default, the sampler for a `dcat` node should calculate the log probability for all possible values of Z[i] and choose from amongst the possible values based on that log probability - i.e., a conjugate sampler in the discrete space.

-chris

  # Prior for Survival
  mean.sj <http://mean.sj> ~ dunif(0, 1)
  mean.sa <http://mean.sa> ~ dunif(0, 1)

  # Priors for Fecundity
  for(t in 1:nyear){
    mean.f[1,t] ~ dunif(0, 1)
    mean.f[2,t] ~ dunif(0, 4)
    mean.f[3,t] ~ dunif(0, 4)
  }

  # Likelihood
  # Model for the initial population size: uniform priors
  for(a in 1:ageclass){
    N[a,1] ~ dunif(100, 2000) # All 3 age classes
  }

  # Process Model
  for(t in 2:nyear){
    N[1,t] ~ dpois(round(((N[1,t-1] - Hf[t-1]) * mean.f[1,t-1] / 2 * mean.sj <http://mean.sj>) +
                          (N[2,t-1] * mean.f[2,t-1] / 2 * mean.sa <http://mean.sa>) +
                          (N[3,t-1] * mean.f[3,t-1] / 2 * mean.sa <http://mean.sa>)))
    N[2,t] ~ dbinom(mean.sj <http://mean.sj>, round(N[1,t-1] - Hf[t-1]))
    N[3,t] ~ dbinom(mean.sa <http://mean.sa>, round(N[2,t-1]- Hyrl[t-1] + N[3,t-1]- Had[t-1]))
  }

  # Observation process for the abundance estimates with their SEs
  for(t in 1:nyear){
    Nhat[t] ~ dnorm(ystar[t], tau.se <http://tau.se>[t])
    tau.se <http://tau.se>[t] <- 1/var.Nhat[t]          # Assumed known and given by variance of Nhat
    ystar[t] ~ dnorm(N[1,t]+N[2,t]+N[3,t], tau.ystar)
  }

  # Recruitment
  for(i in 1:nind){
    J[i] ~ dpois(mean.f[age[i], year[i]])
  }

  # Derived parameters
  # Annual population growth rate
  for (t in 1:(nyear-1)){
    ann.growth.rate[t] <- (N[1,t+1] + N[2,t+1] + N[3,t+1]) / (N[1,t] + N[2,t] + N[3,t])
  }
  # Total population size
  for (t in 1:nyear){
    Ntot[t] <- N[1,t] + N[2,t] + N[3,t]
  }
})
nimdata = list(J = f$Fetus.Count, Nhat = D$abundace, var.Nhat = D$var,
               Hf = c(rep(0, times = 17), hcopy$n[which(hcopy$ageclass == 1)]),
               Hyrl = c(rep(0, times = 17), hcopy$n[which(hcopy$ageclass == 2)]),
               Had = c(rep(0, times = 17), hcopy$n[which(hcopy$ageclass == 3)]))

So I did try to implement some of the suggestion you where mentioning, but none of them solve the problem.

The posterior values for the variable 'r', although not centeredat the true ones, are not at any degenerate value ether. They are just wrong. Also, looking at one of the frozen variables it does not seem that the other value would have been "terrible". I also considered this option and kind of though of a theoretical reasoning for it, but then looking at the values this is not the case.

To give an example here is a flip of the frozen variable:

> Cmodel_param$getLogProb("Z[1]")
[1] -0.2306881
> Cmodel_param$Z[1] ### value was 2
[1] 2
> Cmodel_param$Z[1]<-1
> Cmodel_param$Z[1]
[1] 1
> Cmodel_param$calculate()
[1] -4222.443
> Cmodel_param$getLogProb("Z[1]")
[1] -1.579816
> exp(-0.2306881)
[1] 0.7939871
> exp(-1.579816)
[1] 0.206013

So from the output it does not seem to be a case where "Z[1]| rest of params" is a sort of dirac. Is there a way to see the proposal of the algorithm at the different steps? Or to kind of implement step by step its sample generation mechanism to see where the bug(I think after this evidence it has to be a bug) could be?

messages.body_plain:
I am interested in using nimbleEcology to fit Nmixture models by MLE, and began playing around with a toy example to try to learn the ropes. A few questions cropped up for me.

1.      Does it matter if the model code includes priors, even though they are not used (I think). In the occupancy example at (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/nimbleEcology/vignettes/Introduction_to_nimbleEcology.html it looks like priors are included in the model.

2.      In my toy example, when I return coefficients for p (in the call to optim), or when I return the derived detection probabilities, everything looks OK. But when I try both, the parameter estimates for the coefficients are off, and the hessian has a bunch of zeroes. How can I return both? I fiddled around with the getDependencies function, but couldn’t get it to work the way I expected. I have the same question about the site-level abundances – what if I want to return those?

3.      Is it possible to include random effects, e.g., a random site effect for lambda or p?

I suspect the problem is just my lack of understanding about getDependencies or maybe even my inexperience with optim.

Code for the toy example is attached.

Thanks,

Glenn

messages.subject: Re: Using nimbleEcology to get MLE
messages.subject_clean: Using nimbleEcology to get MLE
messages.body_plain:
Hi Glenn--

Thanks for the questions and glad to see your interest!

1. You should not include priors in the model code when doing MLE. They'll contribute to the log likelihood that's being optimized, which is not what you want. In the vignette we're writing models for MCMC, which we might want to make more explicit.

2. The problem I'm seeing in your code is that you're including "p" in your CalcLogLik function, and providing values for p separately from the values of b1 and b0, which determine p. The only parameters in your model are b0, b1, and lambda, so try just finding maximum likelihood estimates of those. When I fix that on my end, I get sensible estimates and SEs from your first example. In your version that breaks, the optimizer thinks that each "p" is a separate parameter to be estimated. If you want to estimate values of "p" at each site under the model you've written, you can calculate them using the data and the MLE estimates of b0 and b1, but you can't do derived quantities in an MLE setting the way you can in MCMC (and note that the error propagation for those quantities becomes more complicated too).

3. At present, the main way to include random effects when estimating a NIMBLE model with MLE is using the new Laplace approximation feature part of the NIMBLE 1.0.0 release <https://r-nimble.org/version-1-0-0-of-nimble-released-providing-automatic-differentiation-laplace-approximation-and-hmc-sampling>. I'll admit I haven't yet used this new feature so I don't have advice handy, but the NIMBLE User Manual <https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-welcome-nimble.html> is the best place to start for that (Chapter 16.2).

Hope this helps,
Ben

Hello, everyone! I'm playing around with Nimble to see what I can get it to do. I'm trying to construct a relatively simple hierarchical regression model:
```

inits <- list(beta = rep(0,p), tau = .5, phi = phi.mn <http://phi.mn>)
m.nimble <- nimbleCode({

  ## Gaussian data model with mean=mu and Precision matrix = Prec.mat
  y[1:n] ~ dmnorm(mu[1:n], cov = Cov.mat[1:n,1:n])
  for (i in 1:n) {
    mu[i] <- X[i,] %*% beta[1:p]
  }

  ## defining the exponential covariance matrix
  for (i in 1:n) {
    for (j in 1:n) {
      Cov.mat[i, j] <- sigma.sq * exp(-D[i, j] / phi)
    }
  }

  ## Inverse-Gamma prior on sigma-squared
  sigma.sq <- 1 / tau
  tau ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)

  ## Gamma prior on phi
  phi ~ dgamma(a, b)

  ## Exchangeable vague Gaussian priors on each beta[i]
  for (i in 1:p) {
    beta[i] ~ dnorm(0, 0.000001)

})

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,
Thanks for posting and welcome to nimble.
nimble has strict types, including dimensionality, and this can be confusing.
I suspect the issue is that matrix multiplication always returns a matrix, but you are assigning X[i,] %*% beta[1:p] to a scalar.
Two ways to do this are (X[i,] %*% beta[1:p])[1,1] or (what I'd suggest) inprod(X[i,], beta[1:p]).
HTH
Perry

messages.body_plain:
What you've got looks good. One additional thing--the dynamic bounds (Nmin = -1 and Nmax = -1) should only be used in the MCMC context as they can introduce bias in the MLE; the bounds of the truncated infinite sum shouldn't change during MLE. Instead, you should set Nmin = 0 and set Nmax = K where K is some value much higher than the possible maximum abundance at a site. (This is the upper bound of the truncated infinite sum used in likelihood calculation.)

Ben
